my Flask app gives a 500 error after login. traceback says KeyError: 'user_id' in /dashboard. it works on localhost but not on the deployed site behind nginx with https

A KeyError on `session['user_id']` right after login usually means the session cookie isn't coming back. Common causes:

- The cookie is marked `Secure` but the app thinks it's on http.
- `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE` blocks it.
- The SECRET_KEY differs between workers.

Can you check whether the browser stores the session cookie after login?
the cookie is there. I already tried increasing the gunicorn timeout, that didn't change anything

Then the timeout isn't it. With 4 gunicorn workers, a SECRET_KEY generated at startup (`os.urandom`) differs per worker, so a session signed by one worker is rejected by another. That matches "works on localhost" (one process).

Fix: set a fixed SECRET_KEY from an environment variable:

```python
app.config['SECRET_KEY'] = os.environ['FLASK_SECRET_KEY']
```

I'm writing a Python CLI called tidy that cleans my Downloads folder. It must never delete anything, only move files into dated folders.

Good safety rule. I'll use pathlib and shutil.move, and a --dry-run flag that prints moves without doing them.

```python
def plan_moves(folder: Path) -> list[tuple[Path, Path]]:
    return [(f, folder / f'{date(f):%Y-%m}' / f.name) for f in folder.iterdir() if f.is_file()]
```
nice. we decided to use typer for the CLI, not argparse
Typer it is. The entry point becomes `@app.command() def run(dry_run: bool = False)`. I also added a check that skips files still being downloaded (.crdownload, .part).
how do I handle two files with the same name in one month?

Append a counter before the extension: `report.pdf`, `report (2).pdf`, `report (3).pdf`. I wrote `unique_target(path)` that loops until the name is free. It never overwrites an existing file, which keeps your never-delete rule.
can you explain how pathlib glob works with hidden files

`Path.glob('*')` skips nothing by name: on Linux and macOS it includes dotfiles, so `.DS_Store` would be moved. I'd skip names starting with a dot unless you pass --include-hidden. On Windows, hidden is an attribute, not a name, so that check needs `os.stat(...).st_file_attributes`. This matters because macOS writes .DS_Store into every folder you open in Finder, and moving it is harmless but noisy, while on Windows desktop.ini files control folder icons and moving them would change how your folders look. Most cleaning tools skip both by default for that reason, and add a flag for people who really want them moved.

`is_file()` follows symlinks, so a link to a file in another folder would be moved as a link (the target stays put). That's safe, but surprising. I'd skip symlinks by default (`f.is_symlink()`) and log them. Broken symlinks return False for is_file(), so they're skipped already. If you later add a --follow-links flag, be careful: moving the target instead of the link would take files out of the folders they belong to, which would quietly break your never-delete promise in spirit, even though nothing is deleted.
and logging? I want a log of every move

Write one line per move to `~/.tidy/moves.log` as tab-separated `timestamp, source, destination`. That also lets us add an `undo` command later that reads the log backwards and moves files back. Use the logging module with a FileHandler; keep the console quiet unless --verbose. Rotate the log at 5 MB with RotatingFileHandler so it never grows without bound, and write the line only after the move succeeded, so the log never claims a move that didn't happen.

Use pytest with the tmp_path fixture: create fake files with set modification times (os.utime), run plan_moves, and assert the destinations. Test the name-collision case, hidden files, symlinks, and that --dry-run moves nothing. For undo, test that running tidy then undo returns every file to its original path, byte for byte. A property test with hypothesis that generates random file names (spaces, unicode, very long names) catches the edge cases people hit in real Downloads folders.

how should the config file look? I want people to set their own folder names

A small TOML file at ~/.config/tidy/config.toml works well: a `[folders]` table mapping patterns to names, like `pdf = 'Documents'` and `jpg = 'Pictures'`. Load it with tomllib (built into Python 3.11), fall back to defaults when the file is missing, and validate it at startup so a typo shows a clear message instead of a stack trace. Keep the defaults in code so the tool works with no config at all.
what python version should I target

3.11 or newer: tomllib is built in, error messages are much clearer, and it's what most current Linux distributions and Homebrew ship. Declare `requires-python = '>=3.11'` in pyproject.toml so pip refuses older interpreters with a clear message rather than failing later on an import.
how do I package it so I can install it with pipx

Use a pyproject.toml with hatchling as the build backend and a `[project.scripts]` entry `tidy = 'tidy.cli:app'`. Then `pipx install .` from the project folder installs it in its own environment, and `pipx install git+https://github.com/you/tidy` works once it's on GitHub. Keep the package in `src/tidy/` so tests import the installed package, not the working tree, which catches missing files in the build.
the move is slow on my external drive

Moves within one drive are just renames and are instant; across drives, shutil.move copies then deletes, which is slow for big files. Group moves by destination drive, show a progress bar with rich.progress for large batches, and check free space first with shutil.disk_usage so a full drive fails before anything moves. For the never-delete rule this also matters: if a copy fails halfway, shutil.move leaves the source in place, which is the safe outcome.
can it run automatically every day

On macOS use a launchd agent (a plist in ~/Library/LaunchAgents with StartCalendarInterval), on Linux a systemd user timer, on Windows Task Scheduler. I'd add a `tidy schedule` command later that writes the right file for the platform, but start by documenting the three manual setups in the README so people can choose. Always run scheduled jobs without --dry-run only after a first manual dry run.
how do I show what it would do in a nice table

rich.table.Table with three columns: file, from, to. Sort by destination folder so related moves sit together, and truncate long paths in the middle (keeping the file name) so the table stays readable in a normal terminal. Print a one-line summary at the end: 42 files, 5 folders, 1.2 GB, nothing deleted.
some files have no modified date that makes sense

Downloaded files keep the server's timestamp sometimes, so a file downloaded today can claim 2009. Prefer the macOS `kMDItemDateAdded` attribute (via `mdls`) when it exists, then the creation time (st_birthtime), then the modification time.
